extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history (readers interested in World War I and the 1919 Peace Conference)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style overview and critique of the political, social, and diplomatic conditions after World War I, focusing on private enterprise, social unrest, President Wilson's Fourteen Points, and the conduct and composition of the Paris Peace Conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private enterprise should serve the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Private enterprise in 1919 displayed neither will nor capacity for meeting the public needs; business should be a form of public service rather than primarily a method of profit-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues private firms pursued maximum profit—speculation, cornering, luxury production—and failed to meet urgent public needs (housing, road transport, cheap automobiles, shipping). Examples: refusal to convert munition factories into mass-production plants for cheap automobiles, insistence on sale of state-built shipyards, cornering of building materials and rents. The passage urges a change in spirit of business toward social usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speculation and cornering in times of public need
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation, cornering, and luxury production by private enterprise in post-war Europe intensified social and economic disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage cites corners in building materials, rent speculation and sub-letting, and profiteering in rising prices as concrete anti-patterns that exacerbated shortages and dislocation; governments and business failing to restrain these practices risked provoking mass discontent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid amelioration of public discomfort is required to preserve social peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Social peace is impossible without a rapid amelioration of the needless discomforts of the present time; otherwise social revolution becomes likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states that either a rapid resort to willing service and social reconstruction by owning/ruling classes or a worldwide social revolution leading toward equalization of conditions are the alternatives. The choice lies with educated and possessing classes and 'that readjustment cannot be indefinitely delayed; it must come soon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of the changed temper of the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The masses after the war were uprooted, less habituated to acquiescence, and more capable of desperate action; policy must account for their altered temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage notes soldiers and munition-workers had been 'brutalized' by training, were ferocious and less fearful of death, and therefore social unrest was more dangerous than before—policy-makers should not assume pre-war complacency among workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: I — Open covenants and public diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Open covenants of peace openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind, but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the First (and most vital) of Wilson's Fourteen Points; demands transparency in international agreements and the end of secret treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: II — Freedom of navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Absolute freedom of navigation upon the seas outside territorial waters alike in peace and in war, except as the seas may be closed in whole or in part by international action for the enforcement of international covenants."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson's Second Point proposes free seas, though the author notes it is insufficiently comprehensive (questions raised about air-ways and land routes).

rubrics_metrics.name: III — Removal of economic barriers and equality of trade conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general commercial principle intended to reduce economic causes of conflict by promoting open trade among consenting nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: IV — Reduction of national armaments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Adequate guarantees given and taken that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for arms-reduction guarantees to reduce the causes of militarist aggression while preserving domestic safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: V — Impartial adjustment of colonial claims with weight to populations concerned
rubrics_metrics.description: "A free, open-minded and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims based upon a strict observance of the principle that in determining all such questions of sovereignty the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight with the equitable claims of the government whose title is to be determined."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes this as hopelessly vague (no definition of 'claims' or 'title'); it attempts to prioritize indigenous populations' interests in colonial settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: VI — Evacuation of occupied Russian territory and assistance to Russia
rubrics_metrics.description: "A vague demand for the evacuation of Russian territory (then occupied by Germany), and the 'assistance' (undefined) of the Russian people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson's Sixth Point asks for evacuation and undefined assistance—criticized as vague and under-specified for the Russian situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: VII — Evacuation and restoration of Belgium
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for the evacuation and restoration of Belgium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the specific territorial/restorative points addressing wartime occupations and damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: VIII — Evacuation and restoration of French territory, including Alsace-Lorraine
rubrics_metrics.description: "Evacuation and restoration of all French territory, and the 'righting' of the wrong done to France by Prussia in the matter of Alsace-Lorraine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific restitution demand aimed at restoring pre-war borders and addressing historic grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: IX — Readjustment of Italian frontier on lines of nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: "The readjustment of the Italian frontier 'on the lines of nationality.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for border adjustments to follow nationalist principles—one of the national/territorially specific points.

rubrics_metrics.name: X — Autonomy for Austrian subject nations
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Autonomy' of the Austrian 'subject nations.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates self-government/autonomy for peoples within the former Austro-Hungarian Empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: XI — Evacuation of the Balkans and guarantees for Serbia and Balkan independence
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Balkans to be evacuated, Serbia to be granted an outlet to the sea, and the independence of the Balkan States to be guaranteed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial and independence guarantees for Balkan peoples as part of the Fourteen Points.

rubrics_metrics.name: XII — Security and autonomous development for Turkish subject nations; internationalized Dardanelles
rubrics_metrics.description: "Turkish subject nations to be assured of 'undoubted security of life and unmolested opportunity of autonomous development.' The Dardanelles to be internationalized, and Ottoman sovereignty to be recognized only in Turkish districts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for protection and autonomy of non-Turkish peoples within the Ottoman domains and control of strategic waterways.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIII — Polish independence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poland to be independent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific national self-determination point restoring Polish nationhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV — Formation of a general association of nations (League of Nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political and territorial independence for great and small States alike."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The culminating Fourteen Point calling for a League-type international organization to guarantee territorial and political independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wilson's later principles for League constitution and peace (Sept 27, 1918 addenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional statements: the League's constitution must be part of the peace settlement; impartial justice with no favourites; no special or separate interest of a single nation can be the basis of settlement; no internal leagues/alliances within the family of the League; prohibition of special selfish economic combinations or boycotts except where the League itself imposes them; full publicity of all international agreements and treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reproduces Wilson's later speech stressing clarity and detail in the League's constitution and listing five particular requirements (impartial justice, common interest basis, no special enclaves of alliance, economic discipline vested in the League only, full publicity of agreements). It also notes the U.S. willingness to assume responsibilities for maintaining common covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace negotiators should be specially qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of settlement should be entrusted to men specially qualified in geography, ethnology, psychology, political history, etc., rather than to party politicians or mere novices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes the plenipotentiaries as 'merest novices in international affairs' and states that their lack of mastery of key disciplines could have been mitigated by enlisting better-qualified helpers; the passage decries the deliberate choice of 'mediocrities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conducting peace on narrow party lines or personal adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should avoid making the peace settlement an instrument of party advantage or surrounding themselves solely with personal adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson is blamed for conducting the war and peace negotiations on strictly party lines, not incorporating major national figures (e.g., Roosevelt, Taft), and making the issue too personal—this is presented as a grave error that weakened the U.S. role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives should maintain appropriate national/role positioning (not over-personalize)
rubrics_metrics.description: A head of state representing national interests should not personally attend in a way that converts national representation into a personal role; he might better speak occasionally 'as if a nation spoke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues Wilson should have remained in America acting in the role of America rather than coming personally to Paris and thereby personalizing the settlement; the presence of presidential wives and a tourist-like atmosphere are cited as undermining seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace conference should be open, inclusive, and not dominated by a small cabal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Conference ought to be like a frank and open discussion of the future of mankind rather than shrinking into a council dominated by a few (e.g., Council of Four) and resembling an old-fashioned diplomatic conspiracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes the Conference shrank from a Council of Ten to a Council of Four and became less like open discussion and more like a conspiracy; the press and popular journals objected to the 'dictatorship of the group of Premiers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegations and adjoints must be competent and avoid mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plenipotentiaries and their adjoints should be capable, pithy, and well-endowed intellectually—'they deliberately chose mediocrities' is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage emphasizes that although chiefs of state lacked some technical knowledge, this could have been supplied by competent advisors; instead many adjoints were 'gritless and pithless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decorum and seriousness in diplomatic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegations should avoid trivial, tourist, or social behaviors that create a miasma of futility around serious negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes the presence of presidential wives and their tourist-like visits to historical sites during the Conference as introducing a social/tourist quality that undermined the gravity of the settlement.
